description: How two world wars and post-war Labour government expanded the state beyond anything before.
content_html:
The First World War and State Power

Before 1914, the British state was small by modern standards. The Liberal reforms of 1906–11 (old age pensions, national insurance) had begun building a social safety net, but most aspects of daily life were unregulated. The Defence of the Realm Act (DORA), passed just days after war was declared in August 1914, transformed this overnight. DORA allowed the government to requisition factories, control food supplies, censor newspapers, restrict pub opening hours and conscript men into the armed forces.

By 1918 the state had taken control of the railways, the coal mines, parts of the food supply chain, and vast quantities of private property. The total number of civil servants more than doubled during the war. When the war ended, some of this control was relaxed — but the experience had shown that a modern industrial state could, if it chose, direct the economy on a massive scale.

Key Fact

DORA (1914) gave the government powers to requisition factories and property, censor the press, control food supplies, restrict pub hours, and ultimately conscript men. It was the most extensive peacetime-to-wartime expansion of state power in British history to that point.

The Second World War and the Beveridge Report

The Second World War (1939–1945) repeated and deepened the pattern of state expansion. The Emergency Powers (Defence) Act (1939) gave Churchill’s wartime coalition even more sweeping powers than DORA had provided. Rationing, the direction of labour, and the evacuation of children all demonstrated the state’s capacity to organise civilian life. Women entered the workforce in unprecedented numbers — factory work, the Auxiliary Territorial Service, nursing, land work.

In 1942, the economist William Beveridge published his report “Social Insurance and Allied Services.” Beveridge identified five “Giant Evils” in British society: Want, Disease, Ignorance, Squalor and Idleness. He proposed a comprehensive welfare state that would protect every citizen “from the cradle to the grave.” The report sold 600,000 copies and was enormously popular, reflecting a wartime consensus that the sacrifices of ordinary people deserved a better post-war settlement.

In July 1945 the Labour Party under Clement Attlee won a landslide general election, defeating Winston Churchill despite (or perhaps because of) Churchill’s wartime leadership. Labour won 393 seats to the Conservatives’ 213. The result reflected a desire for social change: servicemen and their families wanted the post-war world to be different from the interwar years of mass unemployment and the Great Depression.

Attlee’s government (1945–51) implemented the Beveridge vision: the National Insurance Act (1946) created a welfare safety net for the unemployed, sick and elderly; the NHS was founded on 5 July 1948; the Education Act of 1944 (actually a wartime Conservative measure under R.A. Butler) had already established secondary education for all. The government also nationalised major industries: coal, railways, electricity, gas, steel and the Bank of England passed into public ownership.

The Post-War Consensus

The welfare state and the mixed economy created a post-war consensus: a broad agreement across the major parties that the state had a duty to maintain full employment, fund the NHS, and provide a social safety net. This consensus was not just Labour’s achievement. The 1944 Education Act was Conservative; the Beveridge Report was by a Liberal; Churchill had commissioned it. When the Conservatives returned to power under Winston Churchill in 1951, they did not dismantle the NHS or the nationalised industries — suggesting that the welfare settlement had wide public support.

The consensus began to fracture in the 1970s. Britain joined the EEC in 1973, raising questions about where sovereignty now lay. The “Winter of Discontent” (1978–79) — a period of widespread strikes by public sector workers — damaged the Labour government of James Callaghan and created the conditions for Margaret Thatcher’s election victory in 1979, which would challenge the post-war consensus directly.

Key Fact

The post-war consensus was the cross-party agreement (roughly 1945–1979) that the state should maintain full employment, public welfare, and key nationalised industries. The NHS (1948) and the National Insurance Act (1946) were its centrepieces under Attlee; the Conservatives kept both when they returned to power in 1951.

Britain’s entry into the EEC in January 1973 under Edward Heath’s Conservative government was controversial because EEC membership involved accepting Community law as superior to Acts of Parliament in areas of Community competence (trade, agriculture, competition). This raised fundamental questions about parliamentary sovereignty that had been central to British constitutional thinking since the seventeenth century. The conflict between Parliamentary sovereignty and EEC/EU law became one of the defining political debates of the following four decades.

A referendum on continued EEC membership was held in June 1975 under Harold Wilson’s Labour government; 67% voted to remain. The question of Britain’s relationship with European institutions, and what that meant for parliamentary sovereignty, remained unresolved and highly contested into the twenty-first century.
exam_tip_html: Impartiality note: when writing about the post-war welfare state, frame it as a cross-party achievement, not solely a Labour one. The 1942 Beveridge Report was by a Liberal economist; the 1944 Education Act was a Conservative measure; Churchill’s wartime coalition built the administrative framework. Presenting it as “what Labour achieved alone” misrepresents the historical record and reflects a political bias examiners can identify. Similarly, when discussing EEC entry in 1973, present both sides of the sovereignty argument factually — do not editorially endorse either Eurosceptic or pro-European positions.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • DORA (1914) and the wartime powers of 1939–45 demonstrated the modern state’s capacity to control economic and social life on a vast scale when circumstances demanded it.
  • The Beveridge Report (1942) and Attlee’s government (1945–51) created the NHS, National Insurance and nationalised industries — a post-war welfare settlement with cross-party support.
  • The post-war consensus began to fracture in the 1970s with the oil crisis, industrial unrest and EEC entry raising questions about where power lay and whether the state could deliver its promises.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Defence of the Realm Act (DORA) 1914.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks. Mastering: identifies a specific power (e.g. the government could requisition factories for war production) AND develops it with accurate detail (e.g. this meant private businesses could be compelled to switch from commercial goods to armaments without their owners' consent — a direct extension of state power into private enterprise). Secure: valid feature with limited development. Developing: vague reference to government having more power. Emerging: irrelevant or no attempt.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Beveridge Report (1942).
practice_questions.marks: 2 marks per feature. Mastering: two accurate features each with specific detail (e.g. it identified five 'Giant Evils' — Want, Disease, Ignorance, Squalor and Idleness — as the specific problems a welfare state needed to defeat; it proposed comprehensive national insurance covering all citizens 'from the cradle to the grave' — funded by contributions from workers, employers and the state). Secure: both features with some development. Developing: one feature well described, one vague. Emerging: one vague feature.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the First World War led to a significant expansion of state power in Britain.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: two or more reasons with specific evidence (the scale of the military effort required industrial coordination that the private sector alone could not deliver — DORA allowed requisitioning of factories, food control and conscription; the war required mass mobilisation of civilian workers, including women, blurring the line between civil and military life; total war revealed the state's capacity to direct the economy, setting a precedent; the experience of wartime state action made post-war social reform politically imaginable). Secure: two reasons with some specific detail. Developing: one developed reason or two undeveloped. Emerging: describes DORA without explaining why war expanded the state.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Attlee government's welfare reforms were a cross-party achievement rather than solely a Labour one.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: two or more factors with specific evidence (the Beveridge Report 1942 was by a Liberal economist — Attlee implemented a Liberal plan; the 1944 Education Act was passed by the wartime coalition under Conservative Butler; Churchill's wartime coalition had commissioned the Beveridge Report and built the administrative groundwork; the Conservatives under Churchill in 1951 kept the NHS and nationalised industries, demonstrating cross-party acceptance). Considers why it matters historically that the welfare state was not a purely Labour project. Secure: two factors with relevant evidence. Developing: describes Attlee's reforms without explaining the cross-party context. Emerging: describes the NHS as a Labour achievement without engaging with the question.

practice_questions.text: How significant were the two world wars in changing the role of the state in Britain between 1914 and 1979? [You may consider: DORA; the Beveridge Report; the welfare state; and any other relevant factors.]
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: sustained argument addressing the scale of change (DORA and wartime powers vastly extended state reach; Beveridge and Attlee created permanent welfare institutions; nationalisation created a mixed economy; NHS became central to British life) and continuity/limits (post-war consensus frayed in the 1970s; EEC entry raised sovereignty questions; Winter of Discontent showed limits of state-managed economy; Thatcher's election in 1979 signalled a coming challenge to the consensus). Overall judgement on significance. Secure: argues both sides with relevant evidence; some imbalance. Developing: describes welfare state creation accurately but does not address the question of significance or longer-term limits. Emerging: narrative without addressing the question.

practice_questions.text: Outline the key steps in building the post-war welfare state between 1942 and 1951.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: three or more specific points in sequence (Beveridge Report 1942 — identified Five Giants, proposed welfare state; 1944 Education Act — secondary education for all; Labour landslide 1945; National Insurance Act 1946 — welfare safety net; NHS founded 5 July 1948 — free healthcare; nationalisation of coal, railways, electricity, steel 1946-51). Secure: two or three relevant points with some supporting detail. Developing: one or two accurate points with limited detail. Emerging: vague reference to the NHS being founded.

knowledge_checks.q: What was the Defence of the Realm Act (DORA) and when was it passed?
options: A 1918 Act giving women the vote
A 1914 Act giving the government sweeping wartime powers over the economy and society
A 1939 Act creating the wartime coalition
A 1942 Act proposing a welfare state

knowledge_checks.q: The NHS was founded on 5 July 1948 under which Health Minister?
The Beveridge Report (1942) identified five 'Giant Evils' including Want, Disease, Ignorance, Squalor and _____.
Britain joined the EEC — the European Economic Community — in _____ under Edward Heath's Conservative government.
Match each figure to their role in the post-war settlement:
right: Liberal economist who wrote the 1942 report proposing the welfare state
Labour Health Minister who founded the NHS in 1948
Labour Prime Minister who implemented the welfare state 1945-51

flashcard_questions.q: What was DORA (1914) and what did it allow?
flashcard_questions.a: Defence of the Realm Act — allowed the government to requisition factories, control food, censor press, restrict pubs, and conscript men.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Beveridge call the social problems he identified in 1942?
flashcard_questions.a: The "Five Giant Evils" — he proposed a welfare state to defeat them.

flashcard_questions.q: When was the NHS founded and who founded it?
flashcard_questions.a: 5 July 1948, by Aneurin Bevan as Labour Health Minister.
The cross-party agreement (c.1945-79) to maintain full employment, the welfare state and key nationalised industries.

flashcard_questions.q: Who wrote the Beveridge Report (1942) and what was his political affiliation?
flashcard_questions.a: William Beveridge — a Liberal economist, not a Labour politician.

flashcard_questions.q: Why was the 1945 Labour landslide historically significant?
flashcard_questions.a: Labour won 393 seats and a mandate to build a welfare state — the largest majority in Labour history to that point.

flashcard_questions.q: When did Britain join the EEC?
flashcard_questions.a: January 1973, under Edward Heath's Conservative government.

flashcard_questions.q: What was the Winter of Discontent (1978-79)?
flashcard_questions.a: Widespread public sector strikes under Callaghan's Labour government — damaged Labour's reputation and led to Thatcher's election in 1979.

glossary_terms.definition: The 1914 Act that gave the government sweeping wartime powers to control the economy, suppress opposition, and requisition property and labour.
The 1942 report by Liberal economist William Beveridge that identified the 'Five Giants' of Want, Disease, Ignorance, Squalor and Idleness, and proposed a comprehensive welfare state to defeat them.
The National Health Service, founded on 5 July 1948 by Health Minister Aneurin Bevan, providing free healthcare for all at the point of need — funded by taxation.
The broadly shared political agreement, lasting roughly 1945-1979, that the state should maintain full employment, a welfare safety net, and public ownership of key industries.
The European Economic Community, a trading bloc of Western European nations which Britain joined in 1973 — controversial because it transferred some legislative sovereignty to a European body.
